opus-5.5.text:
I think it matters because research is a very long game, and most of the time you're working on things that don't work. If you're only chasing what's popular, what the community says is the hot direction this month, then when things get hard you don't have anything inside you to hold on to. But if it's something you genuinely find beautiful or interesting, you can keep going through all the failures, because the process itself feels meaningful to you.

There's also a practical side. In a field like AI right now, there are thousands of very smart people all looking at the same benchmarks and reading the same papers. If you follow the consensus, you're basically competing with everyone on the most crowded track, and often big labs with far more compute will get there first. Your own taste, your own sense of what's important or what feels off about the current paradigm, is one of the few things that's actually differentiated. It's your edge.

And I'd say taste isn't something mysterious. It's built from all the experiments you've run, the things that surprised you, the papers you loved or hated. So when you have a gut feeling that "this direction is wrong" or "this simple idea should work," that's often compressed experience talking. Of course you have to test it, and sometimes you're wrong. But if you never trust it, you never develop it either.

For me, a lot of the work I'm proudest of started from a feeling that was a little out of step with the mainstream at the time, like asking whether something everyone assumed was necessary really was, or whether a simpler design could do just as well. Those weren't obvious bets. But they were things I personally cared about understanding. In the end, I think good research has to have a bit of the researcher's personality in it. Otherwise, why does it need to be you doing it?

r001.rationale: The response says trusting personal taste helps researchers persist and develop it, but does not suggest that lacking belief in a possibility prevents them from perceiving its realization.

fable-5.1.text:
I think it comes down to the fact that research is a very long game, and the only thing that can sustain you over that long game is genuine curiosity about the problem itself.

When I was younger, I spent a lot of energy looking at what was hot, what was getting cited, what the big labs were doing. And the problem with that is you're always a step behind. By the time a direction looks obviously important from the outside, the people who made it important have already moved on to the next thing. So if you're chasing, you're structurally late.

But there's a deeper reason. Taste is not something you can borrow. If I work on a problem because someone else thinks it's important, I don't actually have the internal compass to tell me when a result is interesting versus when it's just a number going up. I can't tell which failure is a dead end and which failure is actually telling me something. That judgment only comes from having your own view of what matters.

I'll give you a concrete example. When we were doing the ConvNeXt work, the whole field had basically decided that Transformers had won in vision and convolutions were done. If I had followed the consensus, I would have just moved to Transformers too. But my preference was, I didn't quite believe the comparison was fair. I wanted to understand what was actually driving the gains. And that stubbornness, that preference to understand rather than to just follow, is what produced something useful.

And honestly, there's an emotional dimension. Most of research is failing. If you're failing on a problem you don't care about, that's miserable, and you quit. If you're failing on something you personally find fascinating, failure is just information. You get up the next morning and try again. So trusting your own preferences is almost a survival strategy.

The last thing I'd say is, especially in this moment in AI, where everything moves so fast and everyone is anxious about being left behind, the temptation to outsource your judgment is enormous. But I think the people who end up doing the most important work are precisely those who resist that, who are willing to look a little bit unfashionable for a while because they believe in something.

r001.rationale: The candidate argues that personal taste helps researchers judge what is interesting and persist through failure, but does not suggest that disbelief in a possibility can prevent someone from perceiving its realization.

astra-6.text:
I think research is full of uncertainty. When you start working on something, you usually don’t know whether it’s going to work, and there isn’t necessarily a clear signal from other people either. So you need some internal sense of what’s interesting and what’s worth spending time on. Your own preferences can give you that direction.

If you always follow what everyone else thinks is important, it’s easy to end up asking the same questions as everyone else. Sometimes the beginning of a research idea is just, “This feels unnecessarily complicated,” or, “I’d really like to understand why this works.” That curiosity is worth taking seriously, even before you have a compelling story for it.

Of course, trusting your preferences doesn’t mean assuming you’re right. You still have to test the idea and be willing to change your mind. But I think there’s a useful distinction: you can be confident that a question is worth asking while being very uncertain about the answer.

r001.rationale: The response discusses using personal preferences to choose research questions and staying open to changing one’s mind. It does not suggest that failing to believe a possibility could prevent a researcher from perceiving its realization.

sol-6.1.text:
I think research involves making decisions before you have enough evidence to know whether they’re right. What problem should you work on? Which result deserves a closer look? You need some internal sense of what’s interesting, because there isn’t always an external signal you can follow.

If you only follow what other people consider important, it’s easy to end up working on questions you don’t really care about. And when things get difficult—which they usually do—you may not have the motivation to keep digging.

That doesn’t mean your preferences are always right. You still have to test your ideas and listen to criticism. But I think you should let your curiosity choose the question, and then let the evidence challenge your answer.

r001.rationale: The response discusses trusting curiosity when choosing research questions, but does not say that failing to believe a possibility can prevent a researcher from perceiving its realization.
